question.:question/problem: A saline reservoir for a medical research lab can hold up to $540\,\text{gal}$ of solution. Initially, it contains $270\,\text{gal}$ of saline solution with $36\,\text{lb}$ of dissolved salt. A more concentrated saline solution with concentration $0.4\,\text{lb/gal}$ flows into the reservoir at a rate of $27\,\text{gal/min},$ while the completely mixed solution drains out at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min}.$ Rounded to one decimal place, find the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow.
question.:question/worked-solution:
Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

First, note that a solution containing $0.4\,\text{lb/gal}$ of salt enters the reservoir at a rate of $27\,\text{gal/min}.$ So, the rate at which the *salt* enters the reservoir is 

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (27\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (27\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =10.8\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $270\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $27\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $18\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=270+27t-18t=9(30+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{9(30+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $18\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(18\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{9(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(18\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{9(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{18Q}{9(30+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{30+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =10.8-\frac{2Q}{30+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q=10.8.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(30+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|30+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(30+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(30+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{30+t}\,Q) & =(30+t)^{2}\cdot 10.8 \\ (30+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(30+t)Q & =10.8(30+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2}) & =10.8(30+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(30+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 10.8(30+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(30+t)^{2} & =10.8\cdot \frac{1}{3}(30+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3.6(30+t)+\frac{C}{(30+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the reservoir initially contains $36\,\text{lb}$ of salt. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=36,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =36 \\ 3.6(30+0)+\frac{C}{(30+0)^{2}} & =36 \\ 108+\frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =36 \\ \frac{C}{(30)^{2}} & =-72 \\ C & =-72(30)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3.6(30+t)-\frac{72(30)^{2}}{(30+t)^{2}} \\  & =3.6(30+t)-72{\left(\frac{30}{30+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the reservoir begins to overflow. The reservoir has a capacity of $540\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=540$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =540 \\ 270+27{t}_{o}-18{t}_{o} & =540 \\ 270+9{t}_{o} & =540 \\ 9{t}_{o} & =270 \\ {t}_{o} & =30\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of salt in the reservoir at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(30) & =3.6(30+30)-72{\left(\frac{30}{30+30}\right)}^{2} \\  & =216-72{\left(\frac{30}{60}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈198.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir at time $t,$ the derivative 

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}
$$

describes how this amount changes with respect to time $t,$ in minutes. This is equal to the rate at which salt enters the reservoir minus the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir.

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}
$$

Note that the units of $\frac{dQ}{dt},{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}$ and ${Q}_{\text{out}}^{′}$ are $\text{lb}/\text{min}.$ Now, let's compute the required rates of change in steps.

**Step 1**: Calculating the rate at which salt enters the reservoir.

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{in}}^{′} & =(0.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =(0.4\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}})\cdot (15\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}}) \\  & =6\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 2**: Calculating the rate at which salt exits the reservoir.

To find the rate at which salt leaves the reservoir, we must first determine the volume of solution in the reservoir at time $t.$

The reservoir initially contains $180\,\text{gal}$ of solution; solution enters at $15\,\text{gal/min}$ and mixed solution leaves at $10\,\text{gal/min}.$
As a result, the amount of solution in the reservoir after $t$ minutes is 

$$
V(t)=180+15t-10t=5(36+t)\,\text{gal}.
$$

Note that $V(t)$ is an increasing function, so the reservoir is filling.

Since $Q$ is the amount of salt in the reservoir, the concentration of the solution at time $t$ is

$$
\frac{Q}{5(36+t)}\,\text{lb/gal}.
$$

Therefore, as the completely mixed solution leaves at a rate of $10\,\text{gal/min},$ *salt* leaves at a rate of

$$
\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(10\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(36+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(10\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{5(36+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{10Q}{5(36+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{36+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =6-\frac{2Q}{36+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{36+t}\,Q=6.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(36+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|36+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(36+t)^{2}} \\  & =(36+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}

$$

$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(36+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 6(36+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(36+t)^{2} & =6\cdot \frac{1}{3}(36+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =2(36+t)+\frac{C}{(36+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

$$

$$

\begin{aligned}{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} & =(12\,\frac{\text{gal}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{gal}}) \\  & =(12\,\frac{\cancel{\text{gal}}}{\text{min}})\cdot (\frac{Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\cancel{\text{gal}}}) \\  & =\frac{12Q}{6(15+t)}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}} \\  & =\frac{2Q}{15+t}\,\frac{\text{lb}}{\text{min}}.\end{aligned}
$$

**Step 3**: Calculate the overall rate of change.

The rate of change equals the rate of entry minus the rate of exit. Therefore, 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{dQ}{dt} & ={Q}_{\text{in}}^{′}-{Q}_{\text{out}}^{′} \\  & =9-\frac{2Q}{15+t}\end{aligned}
$$

which gives the equation

$$
\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q=9.
$$

**Step 4**: Integrate the equation.

This is a first-order linear equation with variable coefficients. So we find the general solution using an integrating factor:

$$
\begin{aligned}I(t) & ={e}^{\int 2/(15+t)\,dt} \\  & ={e}^{2\operatorname{ln}⁡|15+t|} \\  & ={e}^{\operatorname{ln}⁡(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Multiplying both sides of the differential equation by $I(t)=(15+t)^{2}$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}(15+t)^{2}\cdot (\frac{dQ}{dt}+\frac{2}{15+t}\,Q) & =(15+t)^{2}\cdot 9 \\ (15+t)^{2}\frac{dQ}{dt}+2(15+t)Q & =9(15+t)^{2} \\ \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2}) & =9(15+t)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, we integrate with respect to $t:$

$$
\begin{aligned}\int \frac{d}{dt}(Q(15+t)^{2})\,dt & =\int 9(15+t)^{2}\,dt \\ Q(15+t)^{2} & =9\cdot \frac{1}{3}(15+t)^{3}+C \\ Q(t) & =3(15+t)+\frac{C}{(15+t)^{2}}.\end{aligned}
$$

We're told that the tank initially contains $18\,\text{lb}$ of flavoring. So, we can apply the initial condition $Q(0)=18,$ and solve for $C:$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(0) & =18 \\ 3(15+0)+\frac{C}{(15+0)^{2}} & =18 \\ 45+\frac{C}{(15)^{2}} & =18 \\ \frac{C}{{15}^{2}} & =-27 \\ C & =-27(15)^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, we obtain the following expression for $Q(t):$

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(t) & =3(15+t)-\frac{27(15)^{2}}{(15+t)^{2}} \\  & =3(15+t)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+t}\right)}^{2}.\end{aligned}
$$

Now, let ${t}_{o}$ be the time when the tank begins to overflow. The tank has a capacity of $210\,\text{gal},$ so we can use the condition $V({t}_{o})=210$ to solve for ${t}_{o}:$

$$
\begin{aligned}V({t}_{o}) & =210 \\ 90+18{t}_{o}-12{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 90+6{t}_{o} & =210 \\ 6{t}_{o} & =120 \\ {t}_{o} & =20\,\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, rounded to one decimal place, the amount of flavoring in the tank at the moment it begins to overflow is

$$
\begin{aligned}Q(20) & =3(15+20)-27{\left(\frac{15}{15+20}\right)}^{2} \\  & =105-27{\left(\frac{15}{35}\right)}^{2} \\  & ≈100.0\,\text{lb}.\end{aligned}
$$
